$comment: The variable-resolution conformance corpus — ONE file, asserted by BOTH
the Rust tests (crates/tropel-core-wasm) and every embedder that hosts a
second implementation of anything on this path.
It exists because a TypeScript re-implementation of this resolver drifted
in two ways that reached the wire silently: a grammar that could not match
a hyphen, and a single raw escape mode where there are three. Both are
pinned below. A corpus is what makes a second host a PORT rather than a
FORK — browsers all implement JavaScript independently and nobody calls
that a fork, because test262 exists.
Shipped in the npm package (see package.json `files`) so an embedder reads
the same bytes rather than copying cases into its own suite, where they
would drift exactly like the code did.
Adding a case: state `why` in terms of the failure it prevents, not what
it does. A case nobody can explain the risk of is a case nobody will

cases.name: hyphenated names resolve
cases.why: A `[\w.:]+` grammar cannot match `-`. This is THE divergence: `{{base-url}}` resolved in a load run and went out as literal text from the embedder.

cases.name: header-style and id-style hyphenated names resolve
cases.why: The two commonest hyphenated shapes in imported Postman collections.

cases.name: names with spaces resolve
cases.why: The grammar is `[^{}]+` — anything but a brace is a name. A charset-based grammar silently excludes shapes like this.

cases.name: dotted and colon-bearing names resolve
cases.why: Colon-bearing keys are how a cached-token reference is spelled; a grammar without `:` left every one of them literal on the wire.

cases.name: json mode escapes quotes so the body stays parseable
cases.why: One raw substitution mode produced INVALID JSON from the embedder and correct JSON from a run of the same collection.

cases.name: json mode escapes newlines and control characters
cases.why: A CSV column carrying a newline is the realistic source; unescaped it truncates the body at the newline.

cases.name: json mode leaves a BARE fragment raw
cases.why: Quote parity: a placeholder inside a string literal is escaped, one standing alone as a value is not. Escaping both would make it impossible to carry a JSON object in a variable.

cases.name: url mode inserts raw
cases.why: Postman does no percent-encoding. Encoding here would mangle a structural URL carried in a variable into one escaped path segment.

cases.name: plain mode does not escape
cases.why: Headers and auth fields want the literal value; JSON-escaping them would corrupt a signature input.

cases.name: an unknown name stays a visible literal
cases.why: Visible, never silently emptied — the user's typo to see. It must NOT be reported as a cycle: an unknown name settles on the first pass.

cases.name: a chain resolves through its links
cases.why: Multi-pass resolution. A single-pass resolver leaves `{{b}}` on the wire.

cases.name: a nested NAME resolves inner-first
cases.why: `[^{}]+` matches only the innermost placeholder. A greedy `[^}]+` matched the OUTER span and could never resolve this.

cases.name: a two-variable cycle is reported, not hung
cases.why: hitCap distinguishes a cycle from an unknown name — both leave a literal `{{…}}`. BOTH names must be reported: the value alternates, so reading names off the final value alone names only one and loses the half that makes the error actionable.

cases.name: a chain deeper than the cap is reported like a cycle
cases.why: The ceiling is one number, read from the resolver — not two constants that happen to agree.

cases.name: a template with no placeholder is returned unchanged
cases.why: The fast path stays fast, and nothing is asked of the resolver when there is nothing to resolve.

cases.name: a value that itself looks like a placeholder is not re-expanded past its own resolution
cases.why: Three links, well inside the cap — pins that the multi-pass loop keeps going rather than stopping after one substitution.
